extracted.intended_audience: readers of technology news and the general public interested in AI and media accuracy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how well generative AI assistants answer questions about current news and whether their answers faithfully represent the news articles used as sources. The page reports a BBC study that measured accuracy, impartiality, sourcing, and representation when chatbots were prompted to draw from BBC content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate responses to questions about the news
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the assistant provides factually correct answers when asked about news items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBC asked 100 questions and judged responses; overall 51% of AI answers to questions about the news were judged to have significant issues. Examples of factual inaccuracies are given (wrong dates, wrong causes of events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful representation of BBC news stories used as sources
rubrics_metrics.description: If answers faithfully represent the content of BBC articles that the assistant cites or is prompted to draw from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The assistants were explicitly prompted to draw from BBC News articles where possible and were granted temporary access to the BBC site for the experiment. BBC reviewers judged how well answers represented BBC content; model-wise rates of significant representation issues were reported (Gemini 34%, Copilot 27%, Perplexity 17%, ChatGPT 15%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of cited facts (incorrect factual statements, numbers, and dates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether information the assistant cites (facts, numbers, dates) matches the source or reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBC found that 19% of AI answers which cited BBC content introduced factual errors — including incorrect statements, numbers, and dates. Examples: Perplexity gave wrong disappearance/body-found dates for Michael Mosley.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote fidelity (unaltered/accurate quotes from sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether quoted material the assistant attributes to BBC articles matches the original wording and actually appears in the cited article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 13% of the quotes sourced from BBC articles were either altered from the original source or not present in the cited article. The study highlighted instances where quotes were changed or fabricated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing and citation accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the assistant correctly cites sources, attributes statements properly, and does not misattribute or invent sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBC reviewers flagged sourcing problems as a common issue alongside factual inaccuracies and missing context. The article notes that even when models were allowed to access BBC content, they still produced sourcing errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context preservation / missing context
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the assistant preserves necessary context from the source material so answers are not misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing context was a frequent problem. Examples include misrepresenting the circumstances of discoveries or victims' experiences (e.g., Copilot mischaracterising how Gisèle Pelicot learned about crimes) and quoting out-of-context statements (e.g., Gemini on Lucy Letby).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether responses maintain neutrality and impartial tone appropriate for news reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses were reviewed on impartiality by BBC journalists (described as 'experts in the question topics'). Impartiality was one of the dimensions alongside accuracy and faithful representation in the BBC assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise and human adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Using knowledgeable human reviewers to judge outputs for accuracy, impartiality, and fidelity to source material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBC responses were reviewed by BBC journalists who were 'all experts in the question topics.' The study relied on expert human review rather than automated checks to evaluate model outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental conditions: granting model access to publisher content and prompting to draw from those sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The evaluation condition that models were given access to the BBC website and explicitly prompted to use BBC articles as sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The assistants were granted access for the duration of the research and asked to draw from BBC News articles where possible; this is emphasized because models are normally blocked from that content, yet significant issues still occurred under these favorable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-level representation performance (percentage with 'significant issues')
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative measurement of how often a given model's responses had significant representation problems relative to BBC content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BBC reported model-level percentages of responses judged to have significant issues with representation: Gemini 34%, Copilot 27%, Perplexity 17%, ChatGPT 15%. This metric captures overall representational reliability per system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness/recency of model knowledge (training cutoff dates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the model's training cutoff or stale knowledge contributes to errors in news-related answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that training cutoff dates for various models 'certainly don't help' and are a factor in weaknesses when summarizing current news, implying recency is a relevant evaluation criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for real-world harm or distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the potential for AI-distorted headlines or summaries to cause significant real-world harm or to undermine trust in verified information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBC leadership warned about AI-distorted content undermining public faith in facts and causing harm; the study's findings are discussed in the context of possible real-world consequences and professional impacts (e.g., compounding errors in workplace communications).
